analysis.one_liner: Orders fast-tracked oil drilling permits in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Interior Department to quickly issue permits for oil and gas exploration and drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, a federally protected wilderness in Alaska. It removes the agency's discretion: the Secretary 'shall' issue the permits promptly. The bill's stated goals are more domestic oil production, government revenue, and jobs. It was introduced in the final weeks of a Congress by one representative, sent to committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that would gain access to drill in the refuge, and Alaska's state government through potential royalties and revenue. The bill's findings claim 55,000 jobs nationwide, $193 billion in new government revenue, and 1.6 million barrels of daily production by 2030 — but these are assertions written into the bill itself, not independently verified estimates.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to 'expediently and promptly' issue permits for energy exploration and extraction in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, opening a protected area to drilling.
The bill's own findings claim drilling would raise Alaskan production to 1.6 million barrels per day by 2030, generate $193 billion in government revenue, and create 55,000 jobs nationwide.
The findings also assert drilling would reduce U.S. dependence on foreign energy and have 'minimal direct environmental impact' — claims stated without supporting evidence in the bill text.

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which holds the Arctic Refuge in trust. Drilling in a wilderness refuge means permanent industrial development of intact habitat for caribou, migratory birds, and polar bears, and added carbon emissions from new oil extraction. The mandate also strips the Interior Department of its usual authority to weigh environmental review before permitting.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public lands trust and wildlife habitat

drawbacks.text: The bill would open a protected wildlife refuge to industrial drilling, a change that is effectively permanent once habitat and infrastructure are in place.
The bill replaces the Interior Secretary's judgment with a mandate to issue permits promptly, short-circuiting the environmental review normally required before drilling on public land.
The economic and jobs figures cited — 55,000 jobs, $193 billion in revenue, 1.6 million barrels a day — appear only as findings written by the bill's sponsor, with no independent analysis attached.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Had it been taken seriously, the tradeoff would have been between the bill's claimed energy and revenue gains and the permanent loss of wilderness habitat in one of the country's most protected landscapes, with the economic claims resting entirely on the sponsor's own assertions. In practice the weighing never happened: the bill went nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to a subcommittee, and with the Congress ending three weeks later, no hearing, vote, or floor action ever followed.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stockman (R-TX) introduced the bill on November 17, 2014, in the closing weeks of the 113th Congress, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day it was introduced.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it remained.
No further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died without a hearing or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic Refuge stayed off the table: with no committee action, no drilling authorization moved, and the refuge's existing protections carried over into the next Congress. Supporters of drilling gained nothing from this attempt, but they lost little, since ANWR opening proposals would return in later Congresses.

for.name: Rep. Steve Stockman
for.role: Sole sponsor, introduced the bill in the final weeks of the 113th Congress
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 5726 and referred it to the Natural Resources Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, passing it to an Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split can be measured; the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have handed drillers access to the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge through mandatory fast-tracked permits. The industry's gain — new drilling acreage — comes directly at the public's cost in protected wilderness and wildlife habitat.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and North Slope oil communities
industries.note: The bill's findings tout production, revenue, and jobs tied to Alaska. Whether those gains materialize and at what environmental cost was never examined, since the bill never advanced.
